description: Team Radiant Orbit builds VAJRA, an ML forecaster (LSTM + Random Forest) using NOAA GOES, ACE Solar Wind, and geomagnetic data to predict radiation belt electron flux. Still evolving, with major upgrades planned during this hackathon as we adapt it for Earth-system trend detection. Looking for ML, full-stack, or Earth/space science teammates to iterate fast with us.
summary: Trend Detective helps anyone answer a simple question: is the Earth changing where I live, and is the change real or just one odd year? A user picks a NASA Earth-science variable, a region and a time span in three guided steps. The app takes monthly NASA data (MERRA-2, GPM IMERG, GLDAS), clips it to the chosen box, computes a latitude-weighted average, removes the seasonal cycle, and tests for a straight-line trend with the Theil-Sen slope and the Mann-Kendall test. These are cross-checked with ordinary least squares and an autocorrelation-aware Hamed-Rao test. It returns a plain-language verdict card, a time-series chart with trend line and confidence band, and an optional per-pixel trend map. Our preloaded results show a clear drying of top-layer soil in the Amazon basin, and only borderline trends for Gujarat temperature and rainfall, because the app flags results that do not survive the autocorrelation check.
details:
What it does: Trend Detective turns NASA monthly Earth data into a verdict a non-expert can read: what is changing, where, by how much, and whether it is statistically significant. It has a guided Q&A, instant demos, and a per-pixel trend map.

Impact: It makes NASA climate data usable for students, teachers and citizens, and it shows uncertainty honestly instead of overclaiming.

Results: Amazon top-layer soil moisture falls by about 0.59 kg/m² per decade (p < 0.001, confirmed by OLS and Hamed-Rao). Gujarat temperature (−0.083 °C per decade) and rainfall (+0.048 mm/day per decade) are labelled borderline.

Tools: Python 3.11, Streamlit, earthaccess, xarray, SciPy, pymannkendall, Plotly; hosted on Streamlit Community Cloud; code on GitHub.

Creativity: a dual-test verdict with built-in honesty warnings, a seasonal-cycle explainer, and a hatched significance map.

Factors we considered: seasonal cycles, latitude weighting, missing values, autocorrelation, natural variability such as El Niño, and the fact that MERRA-2 and GLDAS are model products.

Limitations: only straight-line trends are tested, and the free public server has limited memory, so it serves preloaded demos. Live downloads for other variables run locally. MODIS NDVI and OMI NO2 are planned.
